subject: political-science
lectureTitle: EU II: Institutions of the EU (AUW)
part: Part III · The European Union as a Political System
readings: Bulmer, Parker, Bache, George & Burns (2020), Politics in the EU, 5th ed. · ch. 12, "The Institutional Architecture" (pp. 205 to 237)

cards.front: Which EU bodies are **supranational** and which are **intergovernmental**?
cards.back:
**Supranational** (serve the Union above the states): **Commission, European Parliament, CJEU**.
**Intergovernmental** (they are the states): **European Council, Council of the EU**.

Every EU decision is a negotiation between these two logics: the red thread of the lecture.

cards.front: What is the **European Commission**, and what are its **four jobs**?
cards.back: The EU's **executive and motor**, holding the **right of initiative** (proposes almost all EU law) and representing the Union wide interest. Four jobs: 1) **proposes**, 2) **executes** (manages programmes and funding), 3) **enforces** as **Guardian of the Treaties**, 4) **represents** the EU internationally where it has competence.
cards.hint: The engine with the right of initiative · propose · execute · enforce · represent.

cards.front: What is the **Council of the EU**?
cards.back: The **national ministers** sitting as a legislative chamber, representing member state governments and **colegislating** with the Parliament. It meets in different **configurations** by policy area, with a presidency that rotates among states every six months.

The **summit of national leaders** (the 27 heads of state or government, plus its President and the Commission President). It defines **broad political priorities**, gives **strategic direction**, and resolves major disputes ministers cannot, but it does **not legislate**.

cards.front: Which is the EU's **only directly elected** body, and what are its **main powers**?
cards.back: The **European Parliament (EP)**, the citizens' chamber. It **colegislates** with the Council under the OLP, can **amend or block** law, and **oversees** the Commission, approving it and able to **censure** it.
cards.hint: Elected citizens' chamber; colegislate, amend/block, oversee.

cards.front: Which body is the EU's **supreme court**, and what does it do?
cards.back: The **Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU)**. It **interprets** the treaties and EU law, ensures **uniform application** everywhere, resolves disputes, and **draws the boundary** between EU and national authority.
cards.hint: Top court: interpret, unify, adjudicate, draw the line.

cards.back:
**Exclusive**: **only the EU** may legislate (customs union, single currency, competition rules, common trade policy, fisheries conservation).
**Shared**: **both the EU and the states** may legislate, states acting where the EU has not (internal market, environment, transport, consumer protection).
**Supporting**: **states legislate and the EU only supports or coordinates** (culture, education, tourism).
cards.hint: EU only · both levels · states lead.

cards.front: What three principles **govern the limits of EU competence**: conferral, subsidiarity, proportionality?
cards.back:
**Conferral**: the EU may act **only where the treaties give it competence**; by default power stays national.
**Subsidiarity**: in **nonexclusive** areas, the EU acts **only when the objective cannot be adequately achieved by the states** alone.
**Proportionality**: EU action must **not go beyond what is necessary** to achieve its aim.
cards.hint: Only if conferred · only if better at EU level · no more than necessary.

cards.back:
1) **Commission proposes** (right of initiative). 2) **EP and Council** each examine and **amend**. 3) They **reconcile** versions (often a trilogue with the Commission). 4) **Both approve the same text**. 5) **Adopted**, then implemented and enforced.

Its defining feature is **codecision**: Parliament and Council decide as **equals**, and either can amend or block.
cards.hint: Commission proposes → EP + Council both agree.

cards.back:
A proposal passes with a **double majority**: 1) **55% of member states** (at least **15 of 27**), AND 2) states representing **65% of the EU population**. The 55% protects small states, the 65% protects large ones.

Its radical implication: a government can be **outvoted and still bound**, the sharpest sign the EU is more than an ordinary international organisation.

**Regulation**: **directly applicable**, becomes law in every state **as written**, with no national transposition (strongly supranational).
**Directive**: **binding as to the result** but states must **transpose** it, choosing the means (softer, flexible).
**Decision**: **binding in full on specific addressees** (a state, company or individual), applying directly with no transposition.
cards.hint: Same everywhere · goal binding, states pick the route · binds a named target.

cards.back:
**Positive integration**: EU institutions **build common rules** (legislation, harmonization, standards).
**Negative integration**: EU law **removes national barriers**, often when the **CJEU** strikes down incompatible rules.

One builds, the other clears.
cards.hint: Build common rules vs strike down barriers.
